categories.definition: **Psychedelics** (also known as serotonergic hallucinogens) are a subclass of hallucinogen that produce changes in perception, emotion, and thought while typically leaving the user aware that the experience is drug-induced. They are thought to produce their effects mainly by switching on a particular serotonin receptor known as 5-HT2A, which loosens the brain's usual filtering of incoming information. Common effects include intensified colour, flowing geometric patterns, deepened emotion, and a sense of insight. The term was coined in 1956 from the Greek *psyche* ("mind") and *delos* ("to reveal"), meaning "mind-manifesting."
categories.label: Psychedelic

categories.definition: **Dissociatives** are a subclass of hallucinogen that produce feelings of detachment from one's body, sense of self, and surroundings. They are thought to produce their effects mainly by blocking NMDA receptors, part of the glutamate system the brain uses to bind sensory information and the self into a single coherent experience; interrupting this is what creates the sense of disconnection. Effects range from a floaty, dreamlike state at lower doses to fully immersive out-of-body experiences at higher ones.
categories.label: Dissociative

categories.definition: **Entactogens** (also known as empathogens) are a class of psychoactive substances that produce feelings of emotional openness, empathy, warmth, and closeness to others. They produce their effects largely by triggering a surge of serotonin release, along with some dopamine and noradrenaline, which makes the experience gently euphoric and socially connecting rather than strongly hallucinatory. The term was coined from the Greek *en* ("within"), the Latin *tactus* ("touch"), and *-gen* ("to produce"), roughly meaning "to touch within."
categories.label: Entactogen

categories.definition: **Stimulants** (also known as "uppers") are a class of psychoactive substances that speed up the central nervous system, increasing energy, alertness, wakefulness, and focus while reducing appetite and fatigue. They produce their effects mainly by raising levels of dopamine and noradrenaline, the brain's drive and alertness chemicals, which is also why their effects are often followed by a crash. The name comes from the Latin *stimulare*, "to goad on."
categories.label: Stimulant

categories.definition: **Nootropics** (also known as cognitive enhancers or "smart drugs") are a class of psychoactive substances taken to support mental performance such as memory, focus, learning, and motivation, usually with relatively few side effects. They do not share a single mechanism; different nootropics work in different ways, such as adjusting neurotransmitter levels, increasing blood flow to the brain, or protecting brain cells, so their effects tend to be subtle and gradual rather than producing an obvious high. The term was coined in 1972 from the Greek *noos* ("mind") and *tropein* ("to turn"), meaning "mind-turning."
categories.label: Nootropic

categories.definition: **Antidepressants** are a class of psychoactive medications used to treat depression and related conditions. Most produce their effects by preventing the brain from reabsorbing serotonin or noradrenaline too quickly, leaving more of it active over time, which is why they generally have no immediate effect and take weeks to work. It is worth noting that an antidepressant is not the opposite of a "depressant" drug; the two words use "depress" in different senses, one referring to the mood disorder and the other to the slowing of the nervous system.
categories.label: Antidepressant

categories.definition: **Antipsychotics** (also known as neuroleptics) are a class of psychoactive medications used to manage psychosis, including hallucinations, delusions, and disordered thinking. They produce their effects mainly by blocking dopamine receptors, reducing the dopamine signalling thought to run overactive during psychotic states.
categories.label: Antipsychotic

categories.definition: **Opioids** are a class of psychoactive substances that relieve pain and produce euphoria, relaxation, and contentment, along with sedation and, at higher doses, dangerously slowed breathing. They produce their effects by mimicking endorphins, the body's own painkilling chemicals, and switching on the opioid receptors those endorphins normally act upon. The name comes from *opium*, the extract of the poppy, plus *-oid* ("resembling"); the related term "opiate" refers only to natural poppy derivatives, while "opioid" covers any substance acting on these receptors.
categories.label: Opioid

categories.definition: **Deliriants** are a subclass of hallucinogen that produce a state of delirium marked by confusion, an inability to tell hallucinations from reality, and frequent amnesia of the experience. They produce their effects by blocking acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter the brain depends on for memory, attention, and keeping perception anchored to the real world. Unlike psychedelics and dissociatives, which usually cause hallucinations the user knows are unreal, deliriants tend to produce "true" hallucinations that are indistinguishable from reality, making them the most disorienting of the three subclasses. The name comes from the Latin *delirare*, "to go off the track," originally meaning to stray from the furrow while plowing.
categories.label: Deliriant

categories.definition: **Sedative-hypnotics** are psychoactive substances that commonly cause sedation, drowsiness, or sleep. They include several depressant drug families with different mechanisms of action, including benzodiazepines, barbiturates, alcohol, GABA analogues, and some substances that act through voltage-gated calcium channels. Opioids are categorized separately.
categories.label: Sedative-hypnotics

categories.definition: **Cannabinoids** are a class of psychoactive substances that affect mood, appetite, memory, perception, and pain through the body's endocannabinoid system. They produce their effects by activating the CB1 receptors that the body's own cannabis-like signalling chemicals normally use. Common effects include relaxation, an altered sense of time, and increased appetite. The name comes from the *Cannabis* plant, in which these compounds were first identified.
categories.label: Cannabinoid
